Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes. In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax. Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate. Gov. Gray Davis speaks at an anti-recall labor union rally in San Jose on Oct. 5, 2003. Photo by David McNew, Getty Images In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy. “If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said. But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911. In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.” Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill. “I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change. “The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said. He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms. Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/) would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time. Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed (https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/gov-newsom-announces-position-on-statewide-ballot-propositions/103-a92674ac-c53f-46cf-a625-6e469a288eed) by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021. The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/#:~:text=Bay%20Area%20(51%25).-,Proposition%205,-(Changes%20Recall%20Election), while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes. Where Prop. 5 came from In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office. Weber and good governance groups argued (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/258090?t=338&f=d2d732fccac5f698c6d6489536c70cb8) the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win. They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1), authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/257408?t=362&f=816848bd63bbdd2078deeadec3321c8c) the reform was not needed, would dilute the power of voters and lead to additional special election costs because of the need to hold two elections. Unlike some of the tax measures on the ballot that have spurred multimillion-dollar spending sprees, no group has spent any money on the effort, according to CalMatters campaign finance tracker. Although recalls are often initiated, they rarely make it to voters (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present). Only 11 recalls have made it to the ballot in California since 1913, and only six have been approved by voters. The current recall process is how Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger came into power, replacing Gray Davis in 2003. READ NEXT Democrats want to change the rules for recall elections. Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat. She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.” A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms. If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins. “I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said. California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election. This voter guide has everything you need to know The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections. However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions. The ‘weak gazelle ’ Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman. In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 26 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes. Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax. Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes. In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax. Photo by David McNew, Getty Images In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy. “If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said. But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911. In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.” Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill. “I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat. If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins. “I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said. California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election. This voter guide has everything you need to know The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections. However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions. The ‘weak gazelle ’ Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman. In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 26 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes. Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax. I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms. Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/) would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time. Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed (https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/gov-newsom-announces-position-on-statewide-ballot-propositions/103-a92674ac-c53f-46cf-a625-6e469a288eed) by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021. The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/#:~:text=Bay%20Area%20(51%25).-,Proposition%205,-(Changes%20Recall%20Election), while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes. Where Prop. 5 came from In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office. Weber and good governance groups argued (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/258090?t=338&f=d2d732fccac5f698c6d6489536c70cb8) the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win. They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1), authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/257408?t=362&f=816848bd63bbdd2078deeadec3321c8c) the reform was not needed, would dilute the power of voters and lead to additional special election costs because of the need to hold two elections. Unlike some of the tax measures on the ballot that have spurred multimillion-dollar spending sprees, no group has spent any money on the effort, according to CalMatters campaign finance tracker. Although recalls are often initiated, they rarely make it to voters (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present). Only 11 recalls have made it to the ballot in California since 1913, and only six have been approved by voters. The current recall process is how Republican Gov. Prop. 5: Will California voters change the rules for recall elections?

By Kate Wolffe, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms.

Proposition 5 would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time. 

Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021. 

The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it, while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes.

Where Prop. 5 came from

In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office. 

Weber and good governance groups argued the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win. 

They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. Sacramento State political science professor Kim Nalder was working out at a Sacramento gym in 2003 when she overheard a conversation about the upcoming recall election of then-Gov. Gray Davis, a Democrat. She remembers “guys in the weight room just saying, like, “How cool would that be to have Arnold Schwarzenegger as our governor?’” she said. “It had nothing to do with policy at all.” A few months later, the international action film star triumphed in a field of 135 candidates to replace Davis, who’d been re-elected the year before but had come under fire for rolling blackouts in the state and unpopular vehicle license fees. “The Governator” went on to serve nearly two terms. If the election were just about whether or not Davis should keep his job, and not also who should replace him if he were recalled, Nalder doubts the Republican Schwarzenegger would ever have taken office. Accompanying him on the ballot were a host of other colorful characters, including actor Gary Coleman and porn star Mary Carey. Per the rules of the recall, the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily the majority, wins. “I just think the recall probably wouldn’t have happened — because there wasn’t that much upset at Davis himself — if we didn’t, you know, have any fun alternatives,” she said. California voters this year are deciding whether to approve Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/), which would do away with “the second question” of who should replace a state elected official if they are recalled. Instead, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election. This voter guide has everything you need to know The measure was placed on the November ballot by Democratic lawmakers in 2024 with the support of the secretary of state and good governance groups Common Cause and League of Women Voters. It came in response to the 2021 attempted recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing that it would dilute the power of the voters and add costs associated with follow-up special elections. However, with 14 propositions on the ballot and not a dollar raised so far in support or opposition, both sides may have to rely on voters’ gut reactions. The ‘weak gazelle ’ Aside from the recall of Davis, the only other successful state recall this century was that of the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman. In 2017, Newman was a freshman lawmaker representing a purple Southern California district when he joined 26 of his colleagues in approving the gas tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article143237054.html), which added a 12 cent surcharge to every gallon of gas purchased in California to fund transportation projects. Republicans fiercely opposed the effort, arguing new taxes weren’t necessary. The bill passed with the bare minimum of votes. Less than two weeks later, then-conservative commentator and now-San Diego Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014) told Orange County talk show hosts that gas tax opponents needed to use the “gazelle strategy,” to begin taking out lawmakers who’d approved the tax. Because he was elected by the slimmest margin of any senator, fewer than 2,500 votes. In the ensuing weeks, DeMaio’s organization, Reform California, led the effort to recall Newman, helping to collect more than 64,000 signatures — equivalent to 20% of voters in the last election — and centering its campaign on Newman’s “deciding vote” on the tax. Close to 60% of voters chose to recall Newman in June 2018, replacing him with Republican Ling Ling Chang. The recall ended the Democrats’ supermajority in the state Senate. Gov. Gray Davis speaks at an anti-recall labor union rally in San Jose on Oct. 5, 2003. Photo by David McNew, Getty Images In a recent interview with CalMatters, DeMaio stood by his “weak gazelle” strategy. “If voters want to stop something from happening and being repeated, then mid-term, sometimes the only thing they can do is to use a recall as a way of expressing their opposition,” he said. But Newman said that kind of “political gamesmanship” was not what former progressive governor Hiram Johnson intended when he proposed the law in 1911. In a speech (https://governors.library.ca.gov/addresses/23-hjohnson01.html#:~:text=the%20precautionary%20measure%20by%20which%20a%20recalcitrant%20official%20can%20be%20removed%20is%20designated%20the%20%E2%80%9CRecall.%E2%80%9D), Johnson characterized the recall process as “the precautionary measure by which a recalcitrant official can be removed.” Newman said he doesn’t feel he fit that bill. “I didn’t do anything other than cast a tough vote,” he said. “Was I malfeasant? I hardly think so. Especially given the state of the state’s road systems at the time.” Newman made recall reform one of his priorities when he was elected back into office in 2020. After an expensive recall election (https://calmatters.org/gavin-newsom-recall-election/) for Newsom, other Democrats had the political will and Newman put forward Senate Constitutional Amendment 1, which became Prop. 5. Newman said the title of the proposition, which says that it “Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers,” may confuse voters, since legislators do not hold statewide office, though all California legislative races would be affected by the change. How would it work? If Prop. 5 passes, eliminating the replacement question, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. If they are in the second two years of their term, the lieutenant governor would finish the governor’s term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election. If a statewide official such as the state treasurer, attorney general, or insurance commissioner were recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement to serve until the next scheduled election. If Prop. 5 were to pass, DeMaio said the gap in representation may dissuade voters from approving a recall, even if they want a change. “The argument will now be made, if Prop. 5 passes, that if you vote yes on recall, then you’re going to be without a representative for months, if not longer, and so you’re going to silence your community,” he said. He said extra special elections would lead to higher costs to taxpayers. The 2021 attempted recall of Newsom cost about $200 million to administer — a cost that would double if there were two separate elections. However, Nalder suspects the change would lead to fewer recalls in general, likely a guiding force in Democrats’ support of the effort. “It’s relatively easy to get the signatures, and it causes a lot of chaos and costs a lot of extra money,” she said. “That’s easier for Democrats to want to change because they’re the ones who win more in the races.” A Public Policy Institute of California poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found the measure faces long odds, though: 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote “no” and just 35% said they would vote “yes.” Nalder said the poll was conducted before voters had done their ballot homework, and upon learning more, they’ll likely align with their party’s positions. Proposition 5
Delay replacing recalled state officials
Under current law, after choosing whether to recall an elected official, voters are asked who should replace them. This constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by state lawmakers, would delay the election of a successor until a separate election. The recalled officer would be allowed to run in that election. If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over their duties until a new governor is elected. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.
BEGIN → (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/quizzes)
Support
Oppose
Summary
Support
Proposition 5 is a constitutional amendment born out of a proposal from the secretary of state’s office following the unsuccessful recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. Secretary of State Shirley Weber told lawmakers her office felt a recall election should focus on whether the elected official should be recalled, not whether other potential candidates would be better in the role. Democrat Josh Newman, who was successfully recalled from his state Senate seat in 2018, authored the measure, saying it would reduce the “political gamesmanship” that elevates candidates who otherwise wouldn’t receive a majority of votes.
Oppose
Opponents including the California Republican Party and Election Integrity Project, which advocates for voter ID requirements and restrictions on mail-in voting, argue that allowing the lieutenant governor to assume the governor’s position if the governor were recalled would dissuade people from participating in a recall election. Almost all legislative Republicans also opposed it, arguing that it would dilute the power of voters while protecting incumbents. The current recall process is how former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, was first elected in 2003.

# Prop. 5: Will California voters change the rules for recall elections?
California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms.
Proposition 5 would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office.
If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official.
Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time.
Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024.
It was endorsed by Gov.
Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021.
The outcome of Prop.
5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it, while 52% said they wouldn’t.
The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes.

# Should California Change How It Does Recall Elections?
Of the 14 propositions on the November ballot, quite a few have flown under the radar, including ones that’d change how California conducts recall elections and another to allow public money to finance political candidates.
...
Newsom won in November decisively, with 62 percent of voters rejecting the recall.
But conservative commentator Larry Elder and San Diego’s Kevin Faulconer were also on the ballot as potential replacements if Newsom was recalled.
Elder, who received the most votes among them, could have become governor with only a plurality of the vote had the recall succeeded.
The secretary of state and other Democratic leaders want to change that with Proposition 5.
If it passes, voters would decide first if a state leader or lawmaker should be recalled rather than also the question of who should replace them.
If an official was recalled, there would be a separate special election to replace them, in which the recalled official could also run.
In the case of the governor, the lieutenant governor would be acting governor until the special election.
If the governor were recalled in the final two years of their term, the second in command would serve out the rest of their term.

...
Newsom won in November decisively, with 62 percent of voters rejecting the recall.
But conservative commentator Larry Elder and San Diego’s Kevin Faulconer were also on the ballot as potential replacements if Newsom was recalled.
Elder, who received the most votes among them, could have become governor with only a plurality of the vote had the recall succeeded.
The secretary of state and other Democratic leaders want to change that with Proposition 5.
If it passes, voters would decide first if a state leader or lawmaker should be recalled rather than also the question of who should replace them.
If an official was recalled, there would be a separate special election to replace them, in which the recalled official could also run.
In the case of the governor, the lieutenant governor would be acting governor until the special election.
If the governor were recalled in the final two years of their term, the second in command would serve out the rest of their term.

Proposition 5
Delay replacing recalled state officials
Under current law, after choosing whether to recall an elected official, voters are asked who should replace them. This constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by state lawmakers, would delay the election of a successor until a separate election. The recalled officer would be allowed to run in that election. If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over their duties until a new governor is elected. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.

Support

Summary
Support
Proposition 5 is a constitutional amendment born out of a proposal from the secretary of state’s office following the unsuccessful recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. Secretary of State Shirley Weber told lawmakers her office felt a recall election should focus on whether the elected official should be recalled, not whether other potential candidates would be better in the role. Democrat Josh Newman, who was successfully recalled from his state Senate seat in 2018, authored the measure, saying it would reduce the “political gamesmanship” that elevates candidates who otherwise wouldn’t receive a majority of votes.
Oppose
Opponents including the California Republican Party and Election Integrity Project, which advocates for voter ID requirements and restrictions on mail-in voting, argue that allowing the lieutenant governor to assume the governor’s position if the governor were recalled would dissuade people from participating in a recall election. Almost all legislative Republicans also opposed it, arguing that it would dilute the power of voters while protecting incumbents. The current recall process is how former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, was first elected in 2003.

I'm looking at the opposing case now: the measure would hand the Governor appointment power over statewide seats and take the replacement choice away from voters in that same election. Some opponents frame the proposal as self-protection for Democrats, since the Governor who authored the earlier recall effort is among those affected, and they expect fewer recalls to follow.

I'm checking how the 2018 Newman recall played out, where a Republican replacement was chosen in a concurrent special election with a plurality, which is the kind of outcome Prop. 5's majority rule would change.

I'm now connecting the plurality problem to the 2018 Newman case, where a replacement won with less than a majority. Under Prop. 5, the same seat would instead require a majority, with a runoff if needed.

I'm working through how a majority requirement would play out for legislative special elections, since the top-two runoff should guarantee a majority at the final step. For statewide offices the Governor appoints a replacement, so voters wouldn't weigh in until the next statewide election.

# Prop. 5: Will California voters change the rules for recall elections?
California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms.
Proposition 5 would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office.
If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official.
Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time.
Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024.

The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes.

Delay replacing recalled state officials
Under current law, after choosing whether to recall an elected official, voters are asked who should replace them. This constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by state lawmakers, would delay the election of a successor until a separate election. The recalled officer would be allowed to run in that election. If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over their duties until a new governor is elected. Summary
Support
Proposition 5 is a constitutional amendment born out of a proposal from the secretary of state’s office following the unsuccessful recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. Secretary of State Shirley Weber told lawmakers her office felt a recall election should focus on whether the elected official should be recalled, not whether other potential candidates would be better in the role. Democrat Josh Newman, who was successfully recalled from his state Senate seat in 2018, authored the measure, saying it would reduce the “political gamesmanship” that elevates candidates who otherwise wouldn’t receive a majority of votes.
Oppose
Opponents including the California Republican Party and Election Integrity Project, which advocates for voter ID requirements and restrictions on mail-in voting, argue that allowing the lieutenant governor to assume the governor’s position if the governor were recalled would dissuade people from participating in a recall election. Almost all legislative Republicans also opposed it, arguing that it would dilute the power of voters while protecting incumbents. The current recall process is how former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, was first elected in 2003.

By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 25, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 25, 2026 at 1:16 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Placed on the November ballot by the Legislature, Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/) is billed as a comprehensive reform of state “direct democracy” — an initiative enacted by voters in 1911 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1911_California_Proposition_7) to allow Californians to directly pass laws and remove officials over the objections of powerful interests. But the closer one looks, the more the measure appears motivated by the determination of the Democratic establishment to prevent any Republican or independent from becoming governor through the recall process. This may be fine with many voters, but it shows the proposition is a power play, not a noble endeavor.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most support in a simultaneous vote on the official’s replacement. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger in 2003 was able to quickly replace deeply unpopular Gov. Gray Davis, who had used his executive authority earlier that year to triple (https://www.autorentalnews.com/news/california-triples-vehicle-registration-fee) the state’s vehicle registration fee, mishandled the 2000-01 energy blackouts (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/content/pubs/report/R_103CWR.pdf) and faced disdain even from fellow Democrats like Attorney General Bill Lockyer for his sharp-elbowed “puke politics.” (https://www.ctinsider.com/opinion/article/the-return-of-puke-politics-2512469.php) Nearly 1 million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won in a romp in the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change. He quickly proved more effective than Davis and easily won re-election in 2006.
But if Proposition 5 was then in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante — a Democrat just like all the other lieutenant governors elected since 1982 (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2023/07/lieutenant-rarely-elected-california-governor/). He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in deep blue California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Yes, Schwarzenegger was a unique candidate — a popular movie star with a moderate image. But it is not farfetched to think a self-funded independent candidate with similar views and political skills could do well in a wide-open 2003-style recall replacement vote in California. As both Fox News (http://youtube.com/watch?v=6RGNi_sXd74) and NPR have reported (https://www.nprillinois.org/government-politics/2026-07-27/why-more-candidates-are-running-without-a-party-label), independent candidates have been having an unusually impressive 2026 as millions of voters recoil both from President Donald Trump and the hard-left factions who have made inroads in many state Democratic parties.
The U-T Editorial Board shares the disillusionment of these voters. Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded governors is a bad idea. Vote no on Proposition 5. The status quo has got to go.

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.

Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.

Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

PUBLISHED: September 25, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 25, 2026 at 1:16 PM PDT

Placed on the November ballot by the Legislature, Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/) is billed as a comprehensive reform of state “direct democracy” — an initiative enacted by voters in 1911 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1911_California_Proposition_7) to allow Californians to directly pass laws and remove officials over the objections of powerful interests. But the closer one looks, the more the measure appears motivated by the determination of the Democratic establishment to prevent any Republican or independent from becoming governor through the recall process. This may be fine with many voters, but it shows the proposition is a power play, not a noble endeavor.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most support in a simultaneous vote on the official’s replacement. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger in 2003 was able to quickly replace deeply unpopular Gov. Gray Davis, who had used his executive authority earlier that year to triple (https://www.autorentalnews.com/news/california-triples-vehicle-registration-fee) the state’s vehicle registration fee, mishandled the 2000-01 energy blackouts (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/content/pubs/report/R_103CWR.pdf) and faced disdain even from fellow Democrats like Attorney General Bill Lockyer for his sharp-elbowed “puke politics.” (https://www.ctinsider.com/opinion/article/the-return-of-puke-politics-2512469.php) Nearly 1 million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won in a romp in the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change. He quickly proved more effective than Davis and easily won re-election in 2006.
But if Proposition 5 was then in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante — a Democrat just like all the other lieutenant governors elected since 1982 (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2023/07/lieutenant-rarely-elected-california-governor/). He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in deep blue California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Yes, Schwarzenegger was a unique candidate — a popular movie star with a moderate image. But it is not farfetched to think a self-funded independent candidate with similar views and political skills could do well in a wide-open 2003-style recall replacement vote in California. As both Fox News (http://youtube.com/watch?v=6RGNi_sXd74) and NPR have reported (https://www.nprillinois.org/government-politics/2026-07-27/why-more-candidates-are-running-without-a-party-label), independent candidates have been having an unusually impressive 2026 as millions of voters recoil both from President Donald Trump and the hard-left factions who have made inroads in many state Democratic parties.
The U-T Editorial Board shares the disillusionment of these voters. Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded governors is a bad idea. Vote no on Proposition 5. The status quo has got to go.

By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 25, 2026 at 5:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: September 25, 2026 at 1:16 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Placed on the November ballot by the Legislature, Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/) is billed as a comprehensive reform of state “direct democracy” — an initiative enacted by voters in 1911 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1911_California_Proposition_7) to allow Californians to directly pass laws and remove officials over the objections of powerful interests. But the closer one looks, the more the measure appears motivated by the determination of the Democratic establishment to prevent any Republican or independent from becoming governor through the recall process. This may be fine with many voters, but it shows the proposition is a power play, not a noble endeavor.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most support in a simultaneous vote on the official’s replacement. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger in 2003 was able to quickly replace deeply unpopular Gov. Gray Davis, who had used his executive authority earlier that year to triple (https://www.autorentalnews.com/news/california-triples-vehicle-registration-fee) the state’s vehicle registration fee, mishandled the 2000-01 energy blackouts (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/content/pubs/report/R_103CWR.pdf) and faced disdain even from fellow Democrats like Attorney General Bill Lockyer for his sharp-elbowed “puke politics.” (https://www.ctinsider.com/opinion/article/the-return-of-puke-politics-2512469.php) Nearly 1 million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won in a romp in the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change. He quickly proved more effective than Davis and easily won re-election in 2006.
But if Proposition 5 was then in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante — a Democrat just like all the other lieutenant governors elected since 1982 (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2023/07/lieutenant-rarely-elected-california-governor/). He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in deep blue California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Yes, Schwarzenegger was a unique candidate — a popular movie star with a moderate image. But it is not farfetched to think a self-funded independent candidate with similar views and political skills could do well in a wide-open 2003-style recall replacement vote in California. As both Fox News (http://youtube.com/watch?v=6RGNi_sXd74) and NPR have reported (https://www.nprillinois.org/government-politics/2026-07-27/why-more-candidates-are-running-without-a-party-label), independent candidates have been having an unusually impressive 2026 as millions of voters recoil both from President Donald Trump and the hard-left factions who have made inroads in many state Democratic parties.
The U-T Editorial Board shares the disillusionment of these voters. Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded governors is a bad idea. Vote no on Proposition 5. The status quo has got to go.

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.

Also: Y (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)es or no? Here are the Chronicle’s endorsements for California Supreme Court and appeals courts (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)
Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

But it is there. And the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure.
California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.

Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

When California Governor Gray Davis was the subject of a recall effort in 2003, he said in a televised speech (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.htmlhttps:/www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.html) at UCLA that he thought the recall would damage “the very fabric of our democracy.”
Elected officials may not like to see accountability arrive earlier than expected, but that doesn’t make Californians’ recall powers a threat to democracy.
While Proposition 5 doesn’t attack the people’s ability to hold a recall election, it does tinker with how a replacement candidate is selected.

We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.
